extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism; scholars and critics of Samuel Taylor Coleridge
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for judging authors, poems, and reviews: how to assess originality and borrowing, how reviews should be conducted (tone, purpose, and fairness), and ethical cautions about satire and personal remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality — judge by total result of productions
rubrics_metrics.description: An author is to be judged, in respect of original power, by the total result of his productions. Is the whole something new, or is there in the whole a something new interfused? Can you find the like elsewhere?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate an author's originality across his corpus rather than by isolated passages; look for an overall new quality or infusion that distinguishes the body of work. Avoid over-focusing on isolated resemblances when the total effect is novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of borrowing — acceptability depends on integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost all poets borrow a good deal; there is a difference in the mode of their borrowing: some take the thoughts and images of other writers and combine them with new matter; some take a great deal of what constitutes the substance and brilliancy of their compositions from historical or descriptive books in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish benign borrowing (combining borrowed ideas/images with new material) from excessive borrowing (taking substance and brilliance wholesale). Use examples (Dante, Milton, Gray, Byron, Wordsworth) to judge typical modes; assess whether the borrowings are transformed or merely reproduced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of a good review — expose errors and promote understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: An honest argumentative review, if ever so severe, would have done my Father's works good; a reviewer should expose errors rather than prevent people from attending to an author at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews should aim to clarify and correct, helping readers and the author understand strengths and faults. Severe criticism is acceptable when argumentative and constructive; avoid motives whose aim is to silence or erase an author from consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone of criticism — reasoned not abusive
rubrics_metrics.description: The censures ... are expressed in stern and vehement, but not in coarse or bitter language; they burst forth from a carefully constructed argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer criticism that is argumentative and structured over mere invective. Avoid coarse, bitter, or personally vindictive language; let judgments arise from reasoned argument and evidence rather than abuse or lampooning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making literature subservient to party purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers thought themselves quite at liberty to make the public taste in literature subservient to their own purposes as members of a party; to choke up with rubbish and weeds the streams of public amassus, if a political adversary might be annoyed there!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should not sacrifice literary judgment to party aims. Evaluate works on literary and principled grounds, not as instruments of political warfare; beware of inserting partisan charges that distort literary assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use sweeping unverified charges in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: To bring the most sweeping and frightful charges against their opponents in general terms, whether they had or had not the slightest power to verify them in particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantiate serious accusations with particulars and evidence. Avoid general, unverified aspersions which aim to harm reputation without factual support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire: harm correlates with realism and individual application
rubrics_metrics.description: The wilder and more extravagant a satire appears, the more it contains of devious irrelevant fancy, and the less of individual application... the less harm it does and the less of deliberate malice it shows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess satirical works by how concretely they apply to individuals: wildly extravagant, obviously fanciful satire is less injurious than realistic lampooning that targets persons specifically. When satire verges on realistic depiction of individuals it becomes more harmful and more likely to be malicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about private pointed remarks becoming public
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of these [private remarks] were as strictly true as they were clever; some were just in themselves, but sounded unjust as well as unkind, when repeated unaccompanied by what should have gone along with them to take off their edge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not repeat private, pointed remarks in public without context or mitigating material. Repetition can make otherwise just observations seem cruel; critics and biographers should provide context to prevent misunderstanding or unnecessary harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological analysis of living individuals must be bounded by justice and charity
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological analysis on the living individual subject is an operation that can with difficulty be kept within the bounds of Christian justice and charity; even if we have a right to cut the pound of flesh, how can we be sure of cutting it exactly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or critiquing living persons' characters, exercise restraint and charity; avoid overzealous or forensic dissections that may be unjust or injurious. Prioritize fairness and caution in judgments about motives and inner character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefaces/apologetic writing should be clear and not sophistical
rubrics_metrics.description: The Apologetic Preface ... is an apology in the mode sense of the term; that is an excuse. It contains neither 'metaphysical jargon,' 'unphilosophical sentimentality,' nor 'wire-drawn argumentation', but expresses in clear language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending or explaining work (e.g., in a preface), aim for clarity and honest excuse rather than sophistical defence. Avoid obscure jargon, sentimental posturing, or excessively subtle argumentation that conceals weak grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of examining public conduct and published opinions by principles
rubrics_metrics.description: The first ... consists in examining the public conduct and published opinions of eminent men in the light of principles; not a prejudging of their acts and supposed circumstances made to cast their coloring into error, but an examination of the acts and opinions themselves in due subordination to the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of public figures is legitimate when it examines acts and published opinions against principled standards, not when it unfairly infers motives or constructs smear by conjecture. Keep commentary grounded in documented conduct and stated views, examined by coherent principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mere outward marks from individualizing mental features
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere outward marks for the identifying of the object, as 'letters four do form his name,' are distinct from individualizing features of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In character or authorial study, avoid conflating superficial identifiers (facts, anecdotes) with deep, individualizing features of thought and temperament. Give weight to genuine mental characteristics rather than incidental external marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep principle in view when composing critical prose
rubrics_metrics.description: He ever strove to keep principle in view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should be oriented toward principles (moral, aesthetic, or intellectual) rather than mere party advantage, personal rancor, or ephemeral fashions. Let principled argument guide evaluative judgments.
